<!-- thmalpha-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:A}
    Let $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}\bigl(G,B,(G^{(i)})_{i\in I}\bigr)$
be a residually-connected coset chamber system over the finite type set $I$.  Let $N\trianglelefteq G$ such that $N\cap G^{(J)}G^{(K)}G^{(L)} = \{1\}$ for $J,K,L\subseteq I$. 
Then, for $H\leq N$, $\mathcal{C}/H$ is
residually-connected.
<!-- end thmalpha-1 -->
<!-- thmalpha-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
    For every finite type set $I$, any proper subset $J \subsetneq I$ and any connected graph $\mathcal{G}$ with at least three vertices, there exists a class $2_J$ hypertope whose diagram $\mathcal{D}$ is $\mathcal{G}$ where every edge is labelled by $\infty$. In particular, there exist class $2_J$ two-orbit polytopes of any rank.
<!-- end thmalpha-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the diagram obtained from the graph $\mathcal{G}$ by labeling all edges with $\infty$. Build the Coxeter group $W = W(\mathcal{D})$ and let $\mathcal{C} := \mathcal{C}(W,S)$ be its chamber system. Consider $\operatorname{Br} = \operatorname{Br}(W,S)$, the Brunnian subgroup of $W$. By Theorem \ref{thm:Brunnian-hypertope}, for any subgroup $H \subset \operatorname{Br}$, the quotient chamber system $\mathcal{C}/H$ is a hypertope. By Proposition \ref{prop:AutomorphismGroupQuotient}, the automorphism group of $\mathcal{C}/H$ is isomorphic to $N_W(H)/H$, where $N_W(H)$ denotes the normalizer in $W$ of $H$. Finally, by Theorem \ref{thm:prescribed-normalizer}, there exists such a subgroup $H \leq \operatorname{Br}$ such that $N_W(H) = C_J$. Therefore, $\mathcal{C}/H$ is the desired two-orbit hypertope of class $2_J$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A chamber system $\mathcal{C}$ is \emph{residually-connected} if, for every
$J\subseteq I$ and every family $(Z_j)_{j\in J}$ of pairwise intersecting
$j$-objects, the intersection $\bigcap_{j\in J}Z_j$ is an
$(I\setminus J)$-cell.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:rc-characterisation}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a non-empty connected chamber system over the finite set $I$.
Then $\mathcal{C}$ is residually-connected if and only if, for every chamber $c$ and
all $J,K,L\subseteq I$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rc-cell-identity}
    cJ^*L^*\cap cK^*L^*=c(J\cap K)^*L^*.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:AutomorphismGroupQuotient}
    Suppose that $\mathcal{C}$ is a thin chamber system with automorphism group $G$ and let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ such that $\mathcal{C}/H$ is a thin chamber system. Then, the automorphism group of the quotient chamber system $\mathcal{C}/H$ is isomorphic to $N_G(H)/H$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This is proven in \cite[Proposition 4.2.10]{buekenhout2013diagram} when $\mathcal{C}$ is the chamber system constructed from a Coxeter group. The proof follows the exact same arguments for this more general setting.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:connected-coset-system}
The coset chamber system $\mathcal{C}(G,B,(G^{(i)})_{i\in I})$ is connected if and only if
\[
    G=G^{(I)}=\langle G^{(i)}\mid i\in I\rangle.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:RC_CosetChamberSystem}
Let $I$ be finite, let $B\leq G^{(i)}\leq G$ for every $i\in I$, and assume
that $G=\langle G^{(i)}\mid i\in I\rangle$.  Then the following statements
are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The chamber system $\mathcal{C}(G,B,(G^{(i)})_{i\in I})$ is residually-connected.
    \item For all $J,K,L\subseteq I$,
    $G^{(L)}\cap G^{(J)}G^{(K)}=G^{(L\cap J)}G^{(L\cap K)}$.
    \item For all $J,K,L\subseteq I$,
    $G^{(J)}G^{(L)}\cap G^{(K)}G^{(L)}=G^{(J\cap K)}G^{(L)}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:CoxeterProperties}
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system.  Then
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $J\subseteq I$, the pair $(W_J,S_J)$ is a Coxeter system
    with the restricted Coxeter matrix.
    \item For $J,K\subseteq I$, we have $W_J\cap W_K=W_{J\cap K}$.
    \item For $J,K,L\subseteq I$, we have
    $W_JW_L\cap W_KW_L=W_{J\cap K}W_L$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:acylindrical}
An action of a group $G$ on a metric space $(X,d)$ is \emph{acylindrical} if,
for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exist $R\geq0$ and an integer $N\geq1$ such
that, whenever $x,y\in X$ satisfy $d(x,y)\geq R$, we have
\[
    \bigl|\{g\in G\mid d(x,gx)\leq\varepsilon,
                       \ d(y,gy)\leq\varepsilon\}\bigr|\leq N.
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:loxodromic}
Let $G$ act on a hyperbolic space $X$.  An element $h\in G$ is
\emph{loxodromic} if, for some $x\in X$, the orbit map
\[
    \mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow X,\qquad m\longmapsto h^m x,
\]
is a quasi-isometric embedding.  Explicitly, there are constants
$\lambda\geq1$ and $c\geq0$ such that
\[
    \lambda^{-1}|m-n|-c
    \leq d(h^m x,h^n x)
    \leq\lambda|m-n|+c
    \qquad(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}).
\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:elementary}
Let $G$ act on a hyperbolic space $X$.  Its \emph{limit set}
$\Lambda_X(G)\subseteq\partial X$ is the set of accumulation points in
$\partial X$ of orbits $G \cdot x$.
The action is \emph{elementary} if $|\Lambda_X(G)|\leq2$, and
\emph{non-elementary} if $|\Lambda_X(G)|>2$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:AH}
A group $G$ is \emph{acylindrically hyperbolic} if it admits a
non-elementary acylindrical action on a hyperbolic space.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:WPD}
Let $G$ act on a hyperbolic space $X$.  An element $h\in G$ satisfies the
\emph{weak proper discontinuity condition}, or is a \emph{WPD element},
if, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $x\in X$, there exists an integer
$M\geq1$ such that
\[
    \{g\in G\mid d(x,gx)\leq\varepsilon,
                  \ d(h^M x,gh^M x)\leq\varepsilon\}
\]
is finite.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:EG}
Let $h$ be a loxodromic WPD element for an action of $G$ on a hyperbolic
space $X$.  There is a unique maximal virtually cyclic subgroup of $G$
containing $h$, denoted by $E_G(h)$ and called its \emph{maximal elementary
subgroup}.  It is given by
\[
    E_G(h)=\{g\in G\mid
       g^{-1}h^m g=h^{\pm m}\text{ for some integer }m\geq1\}.
\]
Equivalently, $g\in E_G(h)$ if and only if
\[
    g^{-1}h^m g=h^n
    \quad\text{for some }m,n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Geometrically, $E_G(h)$ is the setwise stabilizer of
$\{h^+,h^-\}$ in $G$.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:commensurable}
Two infinite-order elements $a,b\in G$ are \emph{commensurable in $G$} if
there exist $g\in G$ and $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ such that
\[
    g^{-1}a^m g=b^n.
\]
Otherwise they are \emph{non-commensurable in $G$}.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\cite[Theorem 6.8 and Theorem 7.19, adapted]{DGO}\label{thm:DGO_thms}
    Let $G$ be a group acting on a hyperbolic space $(X,d)$ and let $\{h_1,\ldots,h_k\}$ be a collection of pairwise non-commensurable loxodromic WPD elements of $G$. Then:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item the collection $\{E(h_1),\ldots,E(h_k)\}$ hyperbolically embeds in $G$;
        \item there exists a family of finite subsets $F_i\subseteq E(h_i)\setminus \{1\}$ such that for every collection $N=\{N_i \triangleleft E(h_i)\mid 1\leq i\leq k\}$ satisfying $N_i \cap F_i=\emptyset$, the natural map from $E(h_i)/N_i$ to $G$ is injective for every $1\leq i \leq k$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\cite[Lemma 7.1]{OsinAcylindrical}\label{lem:snormal_non_elem}
    Let $G$ be a group acting acylindrically and non-elementarily on a hyperbolic space $S$. Then every $s$-normal subgroup of $G$ acts non-elementarily.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:quotient-cell-description}
Let $w\in G$ and $J,K\subseteq I$.  Then
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $(HwB)J^* =\{HwxB\mid x\in G^{(J)}\}$;
    \item $(HwB)J^*K^* =\{HwxyB\mid x\in G^{(J)},\ y\in G^{(K)}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:quotient-double-coset-adjacency-simp}, an $i$-adjacency from $HwB$
leads to a chamber of the form $HwxB$ with $x\in G^{(i)}$, and every such
chamber is $i$-adjacent to $HwB$.  Iterating this gives that any chamber reached by a $J$-gallery starting in $(HwB)$ must have the form given in $(a)$. Applying the same argument for the chambers of $(HwB)J^*K^*$ proves $(b)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:correspondenceResidues}
Assume that $N\trianglelefteq G$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:trivial_intersection_N}, and let $H\leq N$.  Fix $w\in G$.  For every
proper subset $J\subsetneq I$, the restriction
\begin{equation*}
    q_H\big|_{(wB)J^*}\colon (wB)J^*\longrightarrow(HwB)J^*
\end{equation*}
is an isomorphism of chamber systems over $J$.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Surjectivity follows from \eqref{eq:J-cell-coset-system} and Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-cell-description}$(a)$.  Suppose that
\[
    HwxB=HwyB
    \qquad(x,y\in G^{(J)}).
\]
Then there exist $h,h'\in H$ and $b,b'\in B$ such that
\[
    hwxb=h'wyb',
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
 h'^{-1}hwx=wyb'b^{-1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
w^{-1}h'^{-1}hw=yb'b^{-1} x^{-1}.
\]
Since $H\leq N$ and $N\trianglelefteq G$, the left-hand side belongs to $N$. As $yb'b^{-1}x^{-1}\in G^{(J)}$, by
Equation~\eqref{eq:one-factor-avoidance} we have $h'^{-1}h=1$, or equivalently $h'=h$. Hence,
$xB=yB$ and thus $q_H\big|_{(wB)J^*}$ is injective.

It remains to show that adjacencies are the same. 
Suppose that $wxB\sim_i wyB$, for $i\in J$ and $wxB,wyB\in (wB)J^*$. Then by the $i$-adjacency of the quotient, $HwxB\sim_i HwyB$.
Conversely, let $i\in J$ and
suppose that $HwxB\sim_i HwyB$.  By
Equation~\eqref{eq:quotient-double-coset-adjacency-simp}, there exist $h,h'\in H$ and
$g,g'\in G^{(i)}$ such that
\[
    hwxg=h'wyg'.
\]
It follows that
\[
w^{-1}h'^{-1}hw=yg'g^{-1}x^{-1}.
\]
As before, this forces $h=h'$, meaning $xg = yg'$.  Hence
$xG^{(i)}=yG^{(i)}$, so $wxB\sim_i wyB$ in $\mathcal{C}$.  Therefore the restriction
of $q_H$ is an isomorphism of chamber systems over $J$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- coro-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:quot_transfer_thin_thick_linearity}
Let $|I|\geq2$, $N\trianglelefteq G$ a normal subgroup that satisfies
the three-factor avoidance condition, and consider $H\leq N$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\mathcal{C}$ is connected, then $\mathcal{C}/H$ is connected;
    \item If $\mathcal{C}$ is firm, thin, or
thick, then $\mathcal{C}/H$ is firm, thin, or thick, respectively;
    \item If $|I|\geq 3$ and $\mathcal{C}$ belongs to a diagram $\mathcal{D}$, then $\mathcal{C}/H$ belongs to the same diagram. In particular, a linear diagram remains linear after taking the
quotient.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end coro-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
$(a)$ The image under $q_H$ of a gallery is a gallery, so connectedness passes to the
quotient.  

$(b)$ For $i\in I$, the singleton $\{i\}$ is a proper subset of $I$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:correspondenceResidues} therefore identifies each
$i$-panel of $\mathcal{C}/H$ with the corresponding $i$-panel of $\mathcal{C}$, proving
that properties such as firmness, thinness, and thickness transfer to the quotient chamber system.

$(c)$ If $|I|\geq3$, each subset $\{i,j\}\subset I$ is proper. Proposition~\ref{prop:correspondenceResidues}
identifies every rank two cell in the quotient with a rank two cell
of $\mathcal{C}$.  Hence, as the Buekenhout diagram is defined on the rank two cells, the diagram itself is
unchanged. In particular, if the diagram is linear, it will remain linear.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:quotient_RC}
Let $ \mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}\bigl(G,B,(G^{(i)})_{i\in I}\bigr)$
be a residually-connected coset chamber system over the finite type set $I$.  Let $N\trianglelefteq G$ satisfy
the three-factor avoidance condition, and consider $H\leq N$.  Then $\mathcal{C}/H$ is
residually-connected.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The quotient chamber system $\mathcal{C}/H$ is connected because $\mathcal{C}$ is connected.  Fixing now a chamber
$c=HwB$ of $\mathcal{C}/H$ and subsets $J,K,L\subseteq I$,  we will prove the identity in
Lemma~\ref{lem:rc-characterisation}.
The direct inclusion is immediate and hence, we will prove the reverse inclusion
\[
    c(J\cap K)^*L^*\supseteq cJ^*L^*\cap cK^*L^*.
\]
 If $J=I$ or $K=I$, this inclusion is also immediate.  Additionally, if
$L=I$, all three sets are the whole quotient chamber system, hence we have trivially the inclusion. 

Let us then assume that $J,K,L\subsetneq I$ and consider $z\in cJ^*L^*\cap cK^*L^*$.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-cell-description}, there exist
$x\in G^{(J)}$, $y\in G^{(K)}$, and $u,v\in G^{(L)}$
such that
\[
    z=HwxuB=HwyvB.
\]
Thus, by the equality of double-cosets, there exists $h,h'\in H$ and $b,b'\in B$ such that
$hwxub=h'wyvb'.$
Rearranging this equality gives
\begin{equation*}
    w^{-1}h'^{-1}hw=yvb'b^{-1}u^{-1}x^{-1}.
\end{equation*}
Since $y\in G^{(K)}$, $vb'b^{-1}u^{-1}\in G^{(L)}$ and $x\in G^{(J)}$, the right-hand side of the 
equality above is an element of
$G^{(K)}G^{(L)}G^{(J)}$. Similar to arguments before, the left-hand side belongs to $N$, and hence, by the three-factor avoidance condition given by Equation~\eqref{eq:trivial_intersection_N},
$h=h'$. Thus, $w^{-1}h'^{-1}hw=1$ and $yvb'= xub$.

As $\mathcal{C}$ is a residually-connected coset chamber system, by Proposition~\ref{prop:RC_CosetChamberSystem}, we have $G^{(J)}G^{(L)} \cap G^{(K)}G^{(L)} =G^{(J\cap K)}G^{(L)}$. Since $yvb'=xub\in G^{(J)}G^{(L)} \cap G^{(K)}G^{(L)}$, we have $yvb'=xub\in G^{(J\cap K)}G^{(L)}$.
Considering Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-cell-description}, this means $z\in c(J\cap K)^*L^*$, finalizing the proof.
Hence $\mathcal{C}/H$ is
residually-connected.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- coro-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a regular hypertope with diagram $\mathcal{D}$ and automorphism group $G := \langle \rho_0,\ldots,\rho_{n-1}\rangle$, with $n\geq 3$. Let $N\triangleleft G$ be a normal subgroup of $G$ such that it satisfies the three-factor avoidance condition. Then $\mathcal{C}/N$ is a regular hypertope with diagram $\mathcal{D}$.
<!-- end coro-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Theorem \ref{thm:quotient_RC} and Corollary \ref{cor:quot_transfer_thin_thick_linearity} show that $\mathcal{C}/N$ is a residually-connected thin chamber system. Since $N$ is normal, Proposition \ref{prop:AutomorphismGroupQuotient} shows that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{C}/N)$ is isomorphic to $G/N$ acting transitively on the coset of $N$ in $G$. Hence, $\mathcal{C}/N$ is chamber transitive, and thus also a regular hypertope. Finally, the fact that the diagrams are equal is shown in Corollary \ref{cor:quot_transfer_thin_thick_linearity}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
The \emph{Brunnian subgroup} of the right-angled Coxeter system $(W,S)$ is
\begin{equation*}
    \operatorname{Br}(W,S)
      :=\bigcap_{i\in I}\ker\bigl(\pi_{I\setminus\{i\}}\bigr).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:pi(Br)trivial}
If $J\subsetneq I$, then
\[
    \pi_J\bigl(\operatorname{Br}(W,S)\bigr)=1.
\]
Equivalently, $\operatorname{Br}(W,S)\leq\ker(\pi_J)$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Choose $i\in I\setminus J$. As $W_J\leq W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$, by
Equation~\eqref{eq:retraction-identities} we have
\[
    \pi_J=\pi_J\circ\pi_{I\setminus\{i\}}.
\]
The map $\pi_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ is trivial on $\operatorname{Br}(W,S)$ by definition, thus the
same is true of $\pi_J$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:Brun_intersect}
Let $J,K,L\subsetneq I$.  Then
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\operatorname{Br}(W,S)\cap W_JW_K=\{1\}$;
    \item $\operatorname{Br}(W,S)\cap W_JW_KW_L=\{1\}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
\emph{(a)} Let $x\in\operatorname{Br}(W,S)\cap W_JW_K$, and write
$x=jk$ with $j\in W_J$ and $k\in W_K$.  Applying $\pi_J$ and using
Lemma~\ref{lem:pi(Br)trivial} gives
    $1=\pi_J(x)=j\pi_J(k)$,
so
\[
    j=\pi_J(k)^{-1}\in\pi_J(W_K)=W_{J\cap K}\leq W_K.
\]
Thus both $j$ and $k$ belong to $W_K$.  Since $K\subsetneq I$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:pi(Br)trivial} also gives
\[
    1=\pi_K(x)=jk=x.
\]

\emph{(b)} Let $x\in\operatorname{Br}(W,S)\cap W_JW_KW_L$, and write
$x=jkl$ with $j\in W_J$, $k\in W_K$, and $l\in W_L$.  Applying the three
retractions and using Lemma~\ref{lem:pi(Br)trivial}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
    j&=\pi_J(l)^{-1}\pi_J(k)^{-1}
       \in W_{J\cap L}W_{J\cap K},\\
    k&=\pi_K(j)^{-1}\pi_K(l)^{-1}
       \in W_{J\cap K}W_{K\cap L},\\
    l&=\pi_L(k)^{-1}\pi_L(j)^{-1}
       \in W_{K\cap L}W_{J\cap L}.
\end{align*}
Choose factorizations
\[
    j=ab,\qquad k=b'd,\qquad l=d'a',
\]
where
\[
    a,a'\in W_{J\cap L},\qquad
    b,b'\in W_{J\cap K},\qquad
    d,d'\in W_{K\cap L}.
\]
Then
\[
    x=a(bb')(dd')a'\in W_{J\cap L} W_{J\cap K} W_{K\cap L} W_{J\cap L}\subseteq W_JW_L.
\]
Part~(a), applied to the proper subsets $J$ and $L$, now gives $x=1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:Brunnian-hypertope}
Let $(W,S)$ be a right-angled Coxeter system of finite rank at least two, and
consider its Coxeter chamber system
\[
    \mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}\bigl(W,(\langle r_i\rangle)_{i\in I}\bigr).
\]
Let $H\leq\operatorname{Br}(W,S)$.  Then $\mathcal{C}/H$ is a hypertope.  If $|I|\geq 3$, it has the same Coxeter diagram as $\mathcal{C}$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The subgroup $\operatorname{Br}(W,S)$ is normal in $W$, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:Brun_intersect}(b) shows that it satisfies the
three-factor avoidance condition \eqref{eq:trivial_intersection_N}, with
$G^{(J)}=W_J$.

Since the Coxeter chamber system $\mathcal{C}$ is connected, thin, and residually-connected, by 
Theorem~\ref{thm:quotient_RC} we have that $\mathcal{C}/H$ is residually-connected,
and Corollary~\ref{cor:quot_transfer_thin_thick_linearity} implies that it is
thin. Hence, it is a hypertope. When $|I|\geq 3$, the diagram follows from  Corollary~\ref{cor:quot_transfer_thin_thick_linearity}(c).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:prescribed-normalizer}
Let $J\subsetneq I$.  There exists a nontrivial proper subgroup $H<\operatorname{Br}$ such that $N_W(H)=C_J$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
If $|I| \geq 3$, then an irreducible right-angled Coxeter group $W$ over $I$ is acylindrically hyperbolic.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
This is a direct consequence of Corollary 2.13 of Minasyan-Osin \cite{minasyan2013acylindrically}. Indeed, the corollary states that an irreducible graph product of non-trivial groups is either virtually cyclic or acylindrically hyperbolic. Any right-angled Coxeter group can be seen as a graph product of groups where each vertex group is cyclic of order two. Beware that the usual convention for graph products is to put an edge to indicate commutation relations. This is the opposite of the convention for Coxeter diagram, where we omit edges to indicate commutation. A graph product is then irreducible when the graph complement is connected. This coincides with our definition of $W$ being irreducible, which is the case by assumption for us. Finally, as soon as $I$ contains at least $3$ elements, the Coxeter group $W$ contains a non-abelian free subgroup, and thus cannot be virtually cyclic. Therefore, $W$ is acylindrically hyperbolic.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:Binfinite}
    If $\Delta$ is connected and $|I| \geq 3$, then the group $\operatorname{Br}$ is an infinite normal subgroup of $W$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The group $\operatorname{Br}$ is normal as it is an intersection of kernels. Suppose for now that $\operatorname{Br}$ is not trivial. Proposition 4.3 of \cite{ParisCoxeter} states that the normalizer $N_W(H)$ of any non-trivial finite subgroup of $W$ must have infinite index in $W$. This directly implies that $W$ cannot have finite non-trivial \emph{normal} subgroups, since their normalizer would be the whole group $W$. Hence, if $\operatorname{Br}$ is non-trivial, it must be infinite.
    
    It remains to show that $\operatorname{Br}$ is not the trivial group. We do so by explicitly constructing an element in $\operatorname{Br}$. Let $ p =p_1-p_2-\cdots-p_{k-1}-p_k$ be a path in the Coxeter diagram $\Delta$ that goes through every vertex, possibly using backtracking. To each $p_i$, let $r_{p_i}$ be the corresponding involution. We construct the nested commutator
    \[
    x := [r_{p_1},[r_{p_2},[\ldots [r_{p_{k-1}},r_{p_k}]]]\ldots]
    \]
    We first show that $x \in \operatorname{Br}$. First of all, every $r_i$ appears at least once since the path $p$ goes through every vertices of $\Delta$. Therefore, deleting any $r_i$ from $x$ creates at least one commutator $[1,y] = 1 = [y,1]$, which then propagates. Hence $x$ becomes trivial after any deletion of a generator, however $x$ is itself non-trivial. Indeed, since we are taking paths along edges labelled $\infty$, no two consecutive generators $r_{p_i}$ and $r_{p_{i+1}}$ will commute. Hence, the expression for $x$ is in the standard normal form for a non-trivial word of graph products.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:existanceLoxodromic}
    There exists a loxodromic $WPD$ element $a \in \operatorname{Br}$ such that $E_W(a) = \langle a \rangle$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Corollary 5.7 of \cite{hull2017small} states that we can find the loxodromic elements with $E_W(a)=\langle a\rangle$ inside any suitable subgroup of $W$. Since we are working with a fixed acylindrical action of $W$, this loxodromic element will automatically be WPD with respect to that action. We thus only need to prove that $\operatorname{Br}$ is a suitable subgroup of $W$. To do so, we first show that the induced action of $\operatorname{Br}$ in non-elementary.

    A subgroup $H < W$ is called $s$-normal if $|H \cap H^g| = \infty$ for all $g \in W$. The subgroup $\operatorname{Br}$ being normal and infinite, it is $s$-normal. By Lemma~\ref{lem:snormal_non_elem}, the induced action of $\operatorname{Br}$ is non-elementary, so that $\operatorname{Br}$ is also an acylindrically hyperbolic group. 
    
    We will now prove that $\operatorname{Br}$ is suitable. 
    Let $K_W(\operatorname{Br})$ be the maximal finite subgroup of $W$ normalized by $\operatorname{Br}$.
    A non-elementary subgroup $H\leq G$ is said to be \emph{suitable} if the maximal finite subgroup of $G$ normalized by $H$ is trivial, that is $K_W(\operatorname{Br})=\{ 1\}$. As $\operatorname{Br}$ is normal, any conjugate of $K_W(\operatorname{Br})$ is also a finite subgroup normalized by $\operatorname{Br}$. By maximality, all the conjugates must be inside of $K_W(\operatorname{Br})$, so $K_W(\operatorname{Br})$ is also normal. As stated in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:Binfinite}, $W$ does not have non-trivial finite normal subgroups. Thus $K_W(\operatorname{Br})=\{ 1\}$ and $\operatorname{Br}$ is suitable.
    We are therefore in the conditions to use Corollary 5.7 of~\cite{hull2017small} and conclude the proof.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
First, we choose some $i \notin J$ and let $r := r_i$ be the associated involutive generator of $W$. Note that $r \notin C_J$. 

By Lemma \ref{lem:existanceLoxodromic}, we can find $a\in \operatorname{Br}$ such that $a$ is a loxodromic $WPD$ element with $E_W(a) = \{g \in W : \exists k,m \neq 0 , g^{-1} a^k g = a^m \} = \langle a \rangle $. Let us define $b := a^r \in \operatorname{Br}$. Since $b$ is a conjugate of $a$, it is also a loxodromic $WPD$ element of $\operatorname{Br}$ with $E_W(b) = \langle b \rangle$. The goal now is to apply Theorem~\ref{thm:DGO_thms} to $\{\langle a\rangle, \langle b\rangle\}$. For that, we need to check that $\{\langle a\rangle, \langle b\rangle\}$ hyperbolically embeds into $C_J$.

First, notice that $a$ and $b$ are non-commensurable in $C_J$. Indeed, for a contradiction, suppose there exists $k \in C_J$ such that 
$$
k^{-1}a^m k = b^n =ra^nr.
$$
Then, setting $g = kr$, we get $g^{-1} a^m g  = a^n$. This implies that $g \in E_W(a) = \langle a \rangle$ and thus $g \in C_J$. However, as $g = kr$ and $k \in C_J$, this would imply $r \in C_J$, a contradiction. 
By the first part of Theorem~\ref{thm:DGO_thms}, the pair $\{\langle a \rangle, \langle b \rangle \}$ hyperbolically embeds into $W$. As $C_J$ is a finite index subgroup of $W$, the pair also hyperbolically embeds in $C_J$.

We can therefore apply the second part of Theorem~\ref{thm:DGO_thms}. Take $N_a = \langle a^{2k} \rangle$ and $N_b = \langle b^{3k} \rangle$ for some sufficiently big integer $k$ that guarantees to avoid the forbidden finite subsets of the hypothesis of the theorem.
Set $H = \langle\langle N_a \sqcup N_b\rangle \rangle_{C_J}$ which is clearly a subgroup of $\operatorname{Br}$. The theorem says that the maps $\langle a \rangle/ \langle a^{2k} \rangle \hookrightarrow C_J / H$ and $\langle b \rangle/ \langle b^{3k} \rangle \hookrightarrow C_J / H$ are both injective. Therefore, in $C_J / H$, the image of $a$ has order exactly $2k$ but the image of $b$ has order $3k$. Therefore, $r$ cannot normalize $H = \langle\langle a^{2k},b^{3k}\rangle\rangle_{C_J}$. Indeed, if that were the case, conjugation by $r$ would go down to an automorphism of $C_J / H$, however it would send an element of order $2k$ to an element of order $3k$, which is clearly not possible.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
